planting.note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Carolina Emerald is a Camellia Forest Nursery introduction selected from small-leaf tea stock that survived a -9F North Carolina winter.

directions: Carolina Emerald is a slow-growing, compact small-leaf tea selection with dark green foliage, bred for reliable performance in cooler parts of the tea-growing range in the American Southeast. Left unpruned it can eventually reach around 10 feet, but regular tipping keeps rows at a manageable 4 to 5 feet, which suits both home harvesting and a tidy hedge planting. Its dense, slow habit makes it a good choice where a smaller, more restrained tea shrub than vigorous large-leaf types is wanted. Give it even moisture and acidic soil, and in the mild winters of the Gulf Coast it should establish and produce without any cold protection.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Alabama Select Tea (Auburn University Commercial Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Alabama Select is the sole surviving named selection from an abandoned Auburn University project to breed commercial tea for Alabama growers.

directions: Alabama Select is an extremely vigorous, upright-branching tea cultivar bred specifically with Deep South growing conditions in mind, making it a natural fit for Gulf Coast gardens. It flowers reliably in fall with the small white blooms typical of the species and tolerates considerably more direct sun than many China-type tea plants, provided soil moisture stays consistent. Its vigor and upright form suit it well to hedge-style harvest rows or a single specimen shrub screened for privacy. As with other tea camellias, keep the root zone acidic and evenly moist and begin light harvesting once the plant is well established.

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Red Leaf is a long-documented Japanese tea type, recorded as far back as 1895, now held in US tea germplasm and breeding collections.

directions: Red Leaf stands out among tea camellias for its distinctly red-tinted new shoots, which contrast with the plant's pink flowers rather than the white blooms typical of most sinensis types. Its new growth also runs noticeably larger-leaved than typical small-leaf China-type tea, giving it an ornamental edge alongside its use for tea harvest. The colorful young foliage makes it worth siting where the spring flush of new growth can be seen up close, such as along a path or near a patio. Provide the same acidic, humus-rich, evenly moist soil as other tea camellias and begin selective harvest of young shoots once the shrub is well established.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service Tea Research

common_name: Chestnut Hill Tea (Morris Arboretum Cold-Hardy Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Chestnut Hill descends from a tea specimen acquired by Philadelphia's Morris Arboretum in 1953 and selected for surviving that USDA zone 7a garden's winter lows.

directions: Chestnut Hill traces to a tea plant growing at the Morris Arboretum near Philadelphia since 1953, a site cold enough to regularly dip well below zero Fahrenheit in winter, and it was propagated specifically because it shrugged off those conditions. That same cold-tested toughness translates into an easy, low-risk choice for the far milder winters of the Gulf Coast, where cold injury is rarely a concern. Grow it as a general-purpose tea shrub for green, oolong, or black tea processing, shaping it into a hedge or specimen as space allows. Maintain the same acidic, evenly moist, humus-rich soil conditions tea camellias need throughout the year.
sources: Morris Arboretum of the University of Pennsylvania
USDA Agricultural Research Service Tea Research

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; MS Oolong is a working selection grown on a commercial Mississippi tea farm and shares nursery-stock ancestry with the Small Leaf tea group.

directions: MS Oolong has been cultivated on a working Mississippi tea farm and processed into oolong-style tea, making it a proven performer under the same hot, humid Deep South conditions found across much of the Gulf Coast. It shares ancestry with small-leaf China-type tea stock, giving it a compact growth habit well suited to hedge-style harvest rows. Because it has already demonstrated it can handle Mississippi's combination of summer heat, high humidity, and occasional cold snaps, it is a reasonable low-risk pick for Gulf Coast zone 8-10 gardens attempting their first tea planting. Keep its soil acidic and evenly moist and begin light harvest of young leaf and bud once the shrub is established.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service Tea Research

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Dragon's Pool descends from Zhejiang, China seed stock planted at Dr. Charles Shepard's Pinehurst Tea Plantation in Summerville, South Carolina, in the 1880s.

directions: Dragon's Pool is among the oldest documented tea selections grown in the United States, tracing back to Zhejiang seed planted at South Carolina's historic Pinehurst Tea Plantation in the 1880s, whose stock went on to supply the Official Hospitality Beverage of South Carolina. Growing it connects a home garden directly to that nineteenth-century lowcountry tea-growing tradition, in a coastal South Carolina climate much like the humid Gulf Coast. Treat it as a standard China-type tea shrub suitable for green, oolong, or black tea processing, pruning to a hedge for easier hand harvest. Maintain acidic, evenly moist, humus-rich soil and expect steady establishment in zone 8-10 conditions.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service Tea Research
